title: Turn a topstitched corner on a sewing machine: needle down by the handwheel, foot up, pivot 90 degrees, foot down
instruction: Turn the corner of the leather panel on the sewing machine, ready to sew its next side.
context: Sewing machine operators and leather goods workers turn corners many times an hour when topstitching bags, wallets, belts and upholstery panels (O*NET 51-6031.00 Sewing Machine Operators). At a corner the operator turns the handwheel by hand until the needle is down through the work, raises the presser foot, pivots the work about the needle until the next side lines up with the feed, then lowers the foot before sewing on. The needle acts as the pivot pin, so the corner stays exactly where the two lines of stitching meet. Turning with the needle up lets the corner shift and breaks the seam line, and in leather every needle hole is permanent, so a stray hole spoils the piece; turning with the foot still down drags and scuffs the work and can bend or break the needle; forgetting to lower the foot leaves the next stitches unclamped.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A single-needle lockstitch sewing machine is set flush in the table and fixed to it, with its needle line at x 25, y 3. Its bed is a gray plate flush with the table (x 17 to 33, y -24 to 7.5) with a steel throat plate (5 x 3.2 cm) around the needle. The off-white cast body has a pillar on the robot's right (x 22.2 to 28.8, y -20.4 to -14, 15 cm tall), an arm across to the left (z 9.8 to 15) and a head over the needle (y 0.4 to 6.2, its underside at z 7.2), with a thread spool on top. The black handwheel (9 cm across, 1.4 cm thick) turns on the pillar's right side about an axis along y, centered at x 25.5, y -21.2, z 12. A black crank knob (2.2 cm across, 2.5 cm long) sticks out to the right from its outer face, 3.3 cm from its center, and starts 60 degrees above the front horizontal (x 23.9, z 14.9). Pushing the knob down turns the wheel's top toward the operator and lowers the needle: the needle goes through the leather once the knob is within 18.5 degrees above horizontal and reaches its lowest at 60 degrees below. The wheel stops 100 degrees above and 95 degrees below horizontal. The steel needle (30 mm stroke) starts with its tip 6.5 mm above the leather. The steel presser foot rests on the leather beside it. The presser-foot lifter is a steel lever 6 cm long pivoting on the head's front face (x 21.8, y -1.4, z 12) and pointing at the robot, with a black plastic grip, 2.5 cm across and 4.2 cm long, sticking out to the right from its end and free to spin (center x 15.9, y -3.8). It has two detents: down (grip 1.2 cm below the pivot, foot down; the start) and up (grip 1.8 cm above it, foot raised 7 mm). The work is a tan leather panel, 16 x 16 cm, 3 mm thick (two glued 1.5 mm layers), 80 g, lying flat on the bed at x 23.5 to 39.5, y 1.5 to 17.5, so the needle is 1.5 cm in from its front-right corner. This is its third corner: cream topstitching (4 mm stitches), 1.5 cm in from the edges, is sewn along its back side and down its right side to the needle, and a scored groove marks the line still to sew along its front and left sides. The panel slides and turns flat on the bed. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run. The needle is in while its tip is at least 1 mm below the leather's underside over the panel; while it is in, the panel can only turn about it. The foot is down only while the lifter lever is in its down detent's zone, where a released lever springs back down; a lever left between the detents holds the foot up. Turns are counted through a 0.05 degree dead band (0.1 mm at the panel's far corner), so the sim's resting jitter never adds up. Score 0, irreversibly, if: the panel turned more than 8 degrees in all while the needle was out of it (turning off the needle); it turned more than 8 degrees in all while the foot was down (dragged under the foot); the needle tip went below the leather's top more than 2 mm from the corner of the stitching, even part way (a stray hole, permanent in leather; 2 mm is half a stitch), or the panel was pushed onto an already lowered needle, moving 1 mm or more in that step (a torn hole); or the panel was forced more than 2 mm sideways while the needle was in (a bent needle). Nothing counts while a hand is still on the work or the machine: a tool point within 3 cm of the lifter lever (its arm or grip) or the knob, or pad tips over the panel within 1.5 cm above it, scores 0. Otherwise, at the end: 1.0 with the panel turned 90 +/- 8 degrees from its start (8 degrees is 1.8 cm over the 13 cm next side, still steered onto the groove in the first stitches), the needle still within 2 mm of the corner and the foot down, both arms back home (each tool point within 3 cm of its start) and still for 1 s; 0.9 the same with the arms elsewhere; 0.75 turned right but the foot left up; 0.5 turned at least 45 degrees about the needle at the corner (halfway); 0.25 the foot was raised with the needle in at the corner and the needle is still in there (raising it again undoes the set-up, so a run put back to its start scores 0); 0 otherwise, including doing nothing. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9 and 1.0. In a real trial, film from above: read the panel's turn with a protractor sheet under the bed, check the needle hole sits on the corner of the stitching, and film the handwheel and the lifter to see the needle was down and the foot up through the whole turn.
reset_notes: Turn the handwheel back until the knob is 60 degrees above the front horizontal (needle 6.5 mm above the leather), lower the foot, and lay the panel back with the needle over the corner of its stitching. A real trial that put a hole off the corner needs a fresh panel.
fidelity: The leather is one stiff 3 mm panel that slides and turns flat on the bed on joints and can't bend, lift or tear. The needle doesn't stitch or carry thread: while it is through, the panel's slides are locked within 0.5 mm, so it only turns about it; a hole is scored from the tip's depth. The foot's grip is heavy damping, not friction. Feed dogs, motor and treadle are not modeled. The lifter, on the back of the head on most machines, is moved to the front for reach.
